A prison guard told me to remove my hoodie before entering the visiting room. I thought it was a security issue. It wasn't.
I visit my brother every two weeks. Eighteen months now. He got three years for something I'm not going to get into. He was twenty-two. Angry. Made a stupid decision that cost him everything.
Mum won't go. Says she can't face it. Dad's been gone since I was twelve. So it's me. Every other Thursday. Same train. Same bus from the station. Same walk up to the gates.
You get used to the routine. Locker for your phone. Clear bag for your coins. Sniffer dog. Pat down. Stamp on your hand. Sit down. Wait.
I was wearing my hoodie because it's what I always wear. It's Thursday. I'm not dressing up to sit in a visiting room on a plastic chair.
I'd been through security a hundred times. Same guards. Same nod. Same wave through.
Thursday the guard didn't wave me through.
"Can you step over here a second?"
My stomach dropped. Something's happened. Something's happened to him. A fight. An incident. They're going to tell me he's in hospital or isolation or worse.
The guard walked me to a side area. Just off the main corridor. Not a room. Just a corner away from the queue.
He looked at my hoodie.
"I need you to take that off."
I started pulling it over my head. Thinking there's a rule I've missed. No hoodies. No hoods. Something.
"No," he said. "Sorry. I don't need you to actually take it off. I just needed you to stop so I could read it properly."
I looked down. "You are enough."
"And the back. I've been trying to read it every visit for three months. You always walk through too fast."
I turned around. Standing in a prison corridor while a guard read the back of my hoodie.
"Dear person behind me, the world is a better place with you in it."
When I turned back he was leaning against the wall. Arms crossed. But not like a guard. Like a man trying to hold himself up.

I was diagnosed with IBS at 19. I'm 34 now. Turns out I never had IBS at all.

For fifteen years, I "managed" a condition I didn't actually have.

Fifteen years of Bentyl that made my mouth so dry I couldn't swallow. 

Fifteen years of peppermint oil capsules that burned coming back up. 

Fifteen years of being handed a prescription and told to "learn to live with it."

I did everything they asked.

I kept a food diary for three years straight. Every meal. Every snack. Every symptom. Every bowel movement. I noted the time, my stress level, where I was in my cycle.

I did the low-FODMAP diet twice. Six weeks of no garlic, no onion, no wheat, no dairy, no apples, no honey. Plain chicken and rice while my husband ordered pizza.

When that didn't work, they tested me for celiac. Negative.

They sent me for a colonoscopy. Clean.

Endoscopy. Normal.

Blood work. Perfect.

"Everything looks fine," my gastroenterologist said. "It's IBS. We've ruled out everything else."

He handed me another prescription for dicyclomine and told me to come back in six months.

I felt like a hypochondriac. Like maybe I was making it up. The tests were normal. The scopes were clean. But every single day, my body told me something was wrong.

By 3pm, my stomach would start to swell. By dinner, I looked six months pregnant. By bedtime, I was on the couch with my jeans unbuttoned, too uncomfortable to move.

Then I'd wake up flat. And the whole thing would start again.

I mapped out bathrooms everywhere I went. Every store. Every restaurant. Every friend's house. I couldn't sit through a movie without knowing my escape route.

I stopped accepting dinner invitations. I never knew if I'd be okay or doubled over in cramps before the appetizers arrived.

I wore elastic waistbands to work because I couldn't predict what size I'd be by noon.

And every doctor just nodded. "That's IBS. Stress makes it worse. Have you tried meditation?"

I tried meditation. I tried yoga. I tried therapy. I tried gut-dir…

Airport security stopped me because of what I was wearing.
Best stop I've ever had.
Flying out of Heathrow. Coming back from a military funeral.
I'm wearing my Live2live hoodie under my jacket because airports are freezing.
Going through security. Officer asks me to step aside.
I'm thinking I'm in trouble.
He goes, "I saw your hoodie when you put your jacket in the tray. What's it say?"
I show him.
"You are enough."
And on the back: "Dear person behind me, the world is a better place with you in it."
He gets quiet.
Then tells me his son's in the Army. Just got back from tour. Won't talk to anyone.
He asks where to buy the hoodie.
Says maybe his son will wear it. Maybe it'll help.
I told him about Live2Live.
How it was started by someone who lost her sister to su!cide.
And that a portion of every sale goes to mental health nonprofits.
He bought 2 hoodies right there, one for him, one for his son.
Then he does something I'll never forget.
Salutes me.
Not for my service. For the hoodie.
Says "Thank you for wearing that. More of us need to."
That wasn't the first time.
Three weeks later. Layover in Edinburgh.
Woman behind me at Costa taps my shoulder.
She's tearing up before she even says anything.
Tells me her brother took his life last year. She's been wearing all black ever since.
She took a picture of the back of my hoodie and sent it to her mum right there.
Two days after that. Gate B7 in Manchester.
Pilot walks up to me. Full uniform.
He doesn't say much. Just points at my hoodie and goes, "I needed to see that today. Thank you."
But it didn't stop there.
Different airports. Different people. Same reaction.
They make these specifically for moments like that.
I travel a lot for work now. Wear this hoodie every single time.
Since that security stop, I've had four more officers, two flight attendants, and a pilot stop me about it.
And every time, I think the same thing.
You never know what they're carrying.
You never know who's standing behind you.

My 4-year-old is still in diapers.

And I genuinely don't understand why.

My name is Bec I'm 31 years old.

Not "won't try."

Won't train.

She's smart. She can read some words. She knows her numbers. 

She follows instructions perfectly.

But potty training? Nothing sticks.

And the confusing part is her younger brother trained at 2 and a half.

No issues. No drama. He just got it.

We first tried when she was 2 and a half.

I read the books. Did the 3-day method. Set aside a long weekend.

Day one was rough. Lots of accidents. But I expected that.

Day two, she seemed to be getting it.

Day three, complete shutdown.

Refused the potty. Held her pee for five hours. Had a meltdown.

I figured okay, she's not ready yet. We'll try again in a few months.

We tried again at 3.

Same pattern. A few days of progress, then total resistance.

Back to diapers.

Tried again at 3 and a half. Same thing.

Every time, it was like hitting a wall.

She'd make a little progress. Then something would shut down. She'd refuse. We'd stop.

I talked to her pediatrician.

She said some kids are more resistant. 

To keep trying.

Stay consistent.

I talked to other moms.

They said maybe she's stubborn. Maybe she needs different rewards. Maybe she has a fear.

I tried everything they suggested.

Different rewards. Special potty seats. Songs. Books. Stickers. Screen time.

Nothing worked.

And then her little brother started showing interest.

He was 2 and a half. Watching her sit on the potty sometimes.

One day he asked to try.

He went. Just like that.

Two weeks later, he was trained.

No meltdowns. No resistance. He just figured it out.

And my daughter? Still in diapers.

I kept thinking there had to be a reason.

She wasn't being stubborn for no reason.

Kids don't refuse to learn something for two years just because.

There had to be something I was missing.

I've sat across the desk from thousands of patients and explained the same things over and over.

Then came the headaches. Mornings mostly, right at the back of the skull, the kind that makes you nauseous.

I'd take my reading first thing and the number would set the mood for my whole day. If it was 145, I was anxious. If it was 155, I was terrified.

I teach at a private school that costs $15,000 a year. Last Thursday, I asked my 6th graders one question: If the Earth spins at 1,000 miles per hour, why don't we fly off? Twenty-three students. Not a single real answer. Their parents are paying for brilliance. We're delivering polished memorization.

I've been teaching for eleven years.

The families at this school are driven. They write a $15,000 check every year because they want their children to be exceptional. They want them to be the sharpest minds in any room.

Last Thursday, I tried something I'd never attempted. A Thinking Quiz. No grades. No right or wrong. Just three questions.

Why is the ocean blue when the water in your glass is clear?

If you're on a spinning planet, why don't you feel it?

Why does the moon seem to chase your car at night?

I watched 23 sixth-graders sit there in silence.

A few of them scribbled down vocabulary words they'd memorized from a textbook. But none of them could actually explain the logic.

Ten minutes later, I picked up the papers.

Lily: "It just is that way."

James: "Gravity???" with three question marks.

Ava: "Because God designed it like that."

Noah: Left his paper completely empty.

These are straight-A kids.

Principal's list.

Already taking pre-algebra.

And not one of them could reason through a basic question for half a minute.

I sat in my classroom during lunch staring at those papers and felt nauseous. These families are spending $15,000 a year. They believe we're building powerful thinkers.

We're not.

We're teaching kids to pass exams. We're producing a generation of children who can look up anything on Google but can't work through a problem on their own for five minutes.

That evening at dinner, I couldn't get those empty papers out of my head.

"Mia, quick one. Why is the sky blue and not purple?"

We take 300g of premium grass-fed beef. We season it with nothing but pure Anglesey sea salt. Then we slowly dehydrate it until just 100g remains.

No sugar. No nitrates. No additives. No fillers. Two ingredients. That's the standard we set for ourselves,  and we've never once lowered it.

👉 Why We Exist

Modern snacking got complicated. Ingredient lists got longer. Labels got harder to read. Somewhere along the way, "high-protein" became code for ultra-processed.
We started Mason's Meats because we believe real food doesn't need 20 ingredients. It needs excellent sourcing, proper craft and zero compromise.

👉 How It's Made

We source 100% grass-fed British and Irish beef from farms we know personally. Family operations. Regenerative practices. Cattle raised on open pasture. Premium cuts selected for flavour, fat balance and texture.

We season with pure Anglesey sea salt from the Welsh coast. Nothing else touches the beef.

Then we dehydrate. Low temperature. Slow process. Small batches. Monitored for texture, bite and fat-to-lean balance every single time.

92% of children in 1957 were potty trained by 18 months.

Today the average is 35 months for girls, 39 months for boys.

What changed? Disposable diapers.

And I'm sitting here absolutely furious because I've wasted over a year waiting for my daughter to show readiness signs that were never going to come.

—

So for the past 14 months everyone kept telling me "wait until she's ready."

My pediatrician gave me this whole checklist of readiness signs to watch for.

Stays dry for 2 hours, shows interest in the potty, can follow simple instructions.

So I waited and watched while she stayed in pull-ups.

And every few weeks I'd think "okay maybe she's ready now?"

But there was always one sign missing so I'd tell myself just wait a little longer.

Month after month after month.

Meanwhile she's 3 and a half and I'm watching 2-year-olds at the playground already trained.

And I'd think "what am I doing wrong?"

But everyone said don't rush it, she'll tell you when she's ready.

So I kept waiting.

For 14 months.

While she stayed comfortable in disposables that I changed 6 times a day.

—

So last week I was scrolling Reddit at 11 PM reading through tips that might help.

And I saw this comment that made me stop cold.

"92% of children in 1957 were toilet trained by 18 months."

Then: "The current average is 35 months for girls, 39 months for boys."

And I'm staring at my phone thinking... wait, WHAT?

Kids used to train at 18 months and now it's past 3 years old?

So I kept reading and the next line actually pissed me off.

"The main reason the average age keeps rising is disposable diapers."

Like the timeline DOUBLED because of diapers?

And I've been sitting here waiting for readiness for over a year while the diapers were the problem the whole time?

So I went down a complete rabbit hole that night.

I found data from the American Academy of Family Physicians.

In the 1940s, training started before 18 months.

Now it starts between 21 and 36 months.

1430215032494054.caption: trysaphire.com
1430215032494054.copy:
My ADHD son's teacher sent me an email that made my stomach drop.

The email came in at 2:27pm on a Tuesday.

"He disrupted the class three times during reading.

He can't stay in his seat.

The other students are struggling to focus around him.

They're starting to leave him out.

He lashes out when he doesn't get his way.

We really need to talk about next steps."

I typed the same reply I'd typed eight times before.

"Thank you for letting me know. We're working on it."

Then I closed my laptop and just sat there. Heartbroken.

My husband came in that night and said what he always says.

"Maybe it's time to just try the medication. Just to see."

My mother-in-law called that weekend.

She didn't say it directly. She never does.

But she said "you know, in my day we didn't have all these options, and kids managed just fine."

Which is her way of saying: why are you making this harder than it needs to be?

But I couldn't explain myself.

Because I knew the medication would work. That was the problem. Stimulants work. I'd been to enough pediatrician appointments to know that.

But I also knew what they cost.

The appetite gone.

The personality quieter than it should be.

The kid who looks like your kid but doesn't quite feel like him.

Another mom in one of my groups described it perfectly: "He was calm, he was focused. But he was not better."

That sentence lived in my head for months.

But I couldn't say that to my husband without sounding like I was making excuses.

I couldn't say it to his teacher without her thinking it was resistance.

I couldn't say it to my mother-in-law without starting a fight I didn't have the energy for.

So I just kept saying: not yet. Just give me a little more time.

And I had no idea how to back that up.

—

She called me in for a meeting.

Sat me down across a table with a printed behavior log.

Three weeks of checkmarks. Every disruption, every redirect, every time he cal…

Potty training pants are a SCAM!!

Who in their right mind would pay $21.00 for underwear??

I’m a full grown woman, I wouldn’t even spend that on my own pants, let alone for a 3 year old…

That’s exactly what I thought before I tried UpAiry training pants.

Now I've changed my mind.

Here’s the thing…

I read the positive reviews, I saw other parents say how they trained in weeks. But I was skeptical. The price just didn’t make sense to me…

So I posted in a Facebook group to ask if anyone had tried them.

The next day I had 10 replies. Here were some of them:

“We wasted months stuck in diapers until I found these”

“My daughter wouldn’t have got into preschool without them”

“My 18 month old is already using the potty”

Even a child development expert replied. “I recommend these to every parent”.

I decided to reply back to her… I wanted to know exactly what made these different from a regular pair of pants.

Here’s what she told me:

1. They aren’t just regular pants. They’re specifically designed to help with potty training.

They provide the sensory feedback your child needs to learn.

They pee in them, they feel the wetness on their skin, their brain gets feedback that something has happened.

Diapers do the opposite. They absorb moisture in seconds. They stay perfectly dry. They could pee in a diaper every day and never feel a thing.

That’s why wearing disposables for too long can make potty training so much harder than it needs to be.

2. They’re a one time purchase.

You think $21.00 is expensive? But how much do you spend on diapers every other week?

You wear them once, you throw them away, you have to buy more.

Training pants are reusable. You buy them once, you wash them, you wear them time and time again.

So they're not expensive, they’re actually a saving.

Only 16% of mothers with young children worked outside the home in the 1950s. Today it's 70%.

And everyone's right—we don't have time to potty train the way they did back then.

Which is why 92% of children in 1957 were potty trained by 18 months.

I work 45 hours a week. I have maybe 3 hours with my daughter on weeknights after pickup.

So I kept delaying. 

"I'll start when I have more time." 
"I'll wait until she's older." 
"I need days off work to do this right."

And now she's 4 years old. Still in diapers. And I'm sitting here absolutely furious.

—

My name is Bec. I'm 31 years old. I work full-time in marketing.

For the past 2 years, everyone kept telling me 

"you need to take time off work to potty train."

"You need 3-5 days straight at home with no interruptions."

"Working moms can't do this the same way stay-at-home moms can."

So I kept waiting for the "right time."

Waiting for a week off. Waiting for her to get older so it would be faster. Waiting for it to somehow get easier.

Meanwhile she turned 3. Then 3 and a half. Then 4.

And I kept thinking "when I have time off work, we'll do it then."

But I never had that time.

And last month, my mother-in-law came over for dinner.

She watched me change my daughter's diaper after bath time.

"You know, in my day, mothers stayed home. My kids were all trained by 18 months."

She didn't say it mean. Just... matter-of-fact.

Like of course I'm struggling. I work. Husband doesn't really help. What did I expect?

Because she's right, isn't she?

If I'd stayed home like my mom did. Like her mom did. Like 84% of moms did in the 1950s.

Maybe this wouldn't be so hard.

719524531147633.caption: aurlux.co
719524531147633.copy:
I saw 4 doctors about my PCOS facial hair. Not one of them asked the question that would've saved me 10 years of suffering….

I sat in my endocrinologist's office, gripping my purse so tightly my knuckles turned white.

This was my fourth doctor in 18 months.

The first one said "It's just PCOS. Try losing weight."

The second told me to "give the Metformin more time."

The third said, "Some women just have more facial hair. It's genetic."

The fourth said, "Have you considered laser? It's expensive but it works."

I was only 29.

Meanwhile, my husband mentioned he was self-conscious about his back hair at his annual physical and walked out with a referral to a dermatologist and three covered options.

One mention. One solution. No shame.

But me?

I was left to silently endure:
✘ Waking up at 5:30am to pluck before anyone saw me
✘ Stubble growing back by noon no matter how thoroughly I removed it
✘ Hair so thick and coarse it felt like wire pushing through my skin
✘ Dark spots spreading across my chin from years of trauma

=====

The nurse called my name.

I exhaled and stood slowly.

"Want me to come in with you?" my husband offered.

I shook my head. "I need to handle this alone."

As I walked down the hallway, one thought pulsed in my mind:

"Please let this doctor actually help me."

=====

Dr. Reyes was different.

She didn't interrupt. She didn't glance at the clock.

She watched as I showed her photos of my chin over the years. How it had gotten progressively worse.

When I broke down and confessed I hadn't worn my hair up in eight years, that I'd missed my best friend's outdoor wedding because I couldn't face being seen in sunlight...

She didn't say, "That's just PCOS."

Instead, she leaned forward and asked something no doctor had ever asked:

"How are you removing this hair?"

I blinked. "What do you mean?"

"Between treatments, between appointments. What's your daily method?"

"I pluck. Every morning. Sometimes twice a day."

She nodded slowly…
719524531147633.description: No wait required. Aurlux works straight out of the box. Apply the 3 step system to clean skin, wait 10 minutes and wipe away. It's that easy.

Genesis 6:4 reads “The Nephilim were on the earth in those days and—also afterward—when the sons of God went to the daughters of humans and had children by them. They were the heroes of old, men of renown.”

Moses writes that In the time of Noah, the Nephilim were on the Earth. It’s the 6th chapter in arguably the most important book of the Bible. Then, right after this, we’re introduced to God's plan to flood the Earth and wipe it clean from all the “evil”

The craziest part of this verse is the “and also afterward.” Implying the Nephilim are STILL on earth to this day, not in physical, but spiritual form!

Genesis 6:6-7 then says, “The Lord saw how great the wickedness of the human race had become on the earth, and that every inclination of the thoughts of the human heart was only evil all the time. 6  The Lord regretted that he had made human beings on the earth, and his heart was deeply troubled. 7 ”

Then, we’re introduced to the parallel of Enoch and Noah. We learn Enoch walked with God, how Noah was blameless, what the Nephilim were, then immediately after, the Great Flood.

Genesis 5:24: “Enoch walked faithfully with God; then he was no more, because God took him away.” Genesis 6:9: “Noah was a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time, and he walked faithfully with God”

I always thought how weird it was that Enoch walked with God, but his book wasn’t included in the King James Bible. I knew the reason too. They weren't able to prove it to be authentic.

“I had Representative Anna Paulina on the podcast, and she was talking to me about the Book of Enoch. She said it wasn’t included in the Bible because a bunch of jewish rabbis said it didn’t align with the Torah, so they yanked it out. But it’s an original biblical text, they found it in the Dead Sea Scrolls”

In 30 years of making the Luxury Hobo Bag, I've learned that women don't want what fashion magazines tell them they want.

They don't want trendy logos that'll be outdated next season.

They don't want complicated designs with 47 pockets they'll never use.

They don't want bags so expensive they feel guilty carrying them.

What they want is simple: a bag that actually works for real life.

I learned this the hard way.

When I first started in 1995, I thought I knew exactly what women needed. I had designed what I thought was the perfect bag—modern, minimalist, and sleek.

I was so proud of it.

Then I gave it to five women to test for a month.

Four of them came back with the same complaint: "Susan, it's beautiful, but I can't find anything inside it."

One woman said, "I spent 10 minutes looking for my car keys in a parking lot. My phone was ringing and I couldn't reach it fast enough."

I was devastated. I'd spent six months on that design.

But that's when I started really listening.

I asked women to show me their bags. To tell me what frustrated them most. What they wished was different.

And I discovered something crucial: the biggest problems weren't about style. They were about function.

Women were tired of bags where everything got lost in one big black hole.

They were anxious about pickpockets, especially when traveling.

Their shoulders hurt from straps that weren't designed properly.

They were exhausted from constantly replacing bags that fell apart.

So I went back to my workshop and started over.

I created organized interior compartments based on what women actually carry. Phone pocket. Wallet slot. Key clip. Sunglasses space. Everything is visible and accessible.

I designed a hidden back pocket after my own sister was robbed on a trip. It sits completely flush against your body where thieves can't reach it, but you can access it easily.

My ex-husband's new wife and I ended up at the same dinner table in Paris for my daughter's thirtieth birthday trip. She didn't know I was coming. I did.

Sophie turned thirty in September. She'd been planning the Paris trip for almost a year. Four days, five friends, a nice hotel in Le Marais.

She asked me months in advance. I told her I'd be there.

What I didn't know was that David had also been invited. With Melissa.

I found out seven weeks before the trip when Sophie called me.

"Mum. I need to tell you something."

"Okay."

"Dad's coming to Paris. With Melissa." A pause. "And Melissa offered to send you some make-up recommendations for the trip. She said Dad mentioned your skin has been looking a bit tired lately, and she wanted to help make sure you felt confident for all the photos."

Dad mentioned your skin has been looking a bit tired lately.

David had commented on my appearance for twenty-two years. Every outfit, every product, every bit of effort I made. Not because I asked him to. Because control was how he expressed love — or what he called love. I had a career in finance, ran our household accounts, raised two kids mostly alone while he travelled for work. I was not a woman who had let herself go.

But I'd let his opinions land. And somewhere in those twenty-two years, hearing them became believing them, at least in the story he told.

And now he'd given that story to Melissa. And Melissa had given it to Sophie.

"I'm fine," I told her. "I'll handle my own skincare."

A day later, Melissa texted me directly.

"Hi Susan! Sophie shared your number — hope that's okay. I've been putting together a little skincare guide for the trip since the Parisian air can be so drying on mature skin. Happy to send it over if useful?"

A skincare guide. She'd made me a skincare guide.

"Thank you, I'm all sorted," I replied.

"Of course! Let me know if anything comes up. I've been doing a ten-step face every morning for years so happy to be a resource 😊"

25222671814055755.caption: florusrelief.com
25222671814055755.copy:
I was on the floor of the bathroom, forehead pressed against the cold tile, when I realised that yet another Migraine has knocked me out. My palms were shaking when I tried to tear open that ridiculous little silver square with the strength of someone losing a race against time. The pain behind my eye was already blooming into something I knew too well: a full-blown migraine. My vision blurred, the nausea rising in waves. And there I was, fighting cardboard and foil like it was a locked safe instead of medicine. Sumatriptan. The so-called lifesaver that never seemed to come fast enough when I needed it.

I used to joke that whoever designed those blister packs had clearly never had a migraine. But it wasn’t funny. Not when your hands are trembling, the light is stabbing your skull, and all you want is the pill that might, maybe, dull the pain if you could just get it out in time. I’ve used scissors, teeth, even keys to pry them open. Once, I actually crushed the tablet in the process. I cried. Not from the pain. From the helplessness.

1948605459875502.copy:
I was diagnosed with Ménière's disease at 51. I'm 58 now. Turns out I never had Ménière's at all.

For seven years, I "managed" a condition without understanding what was actually driving it.

But every year, I felt myself shrinking a little more.

Seven years of diuretics that made me exhausted and dehydrated.

Seven years of low-sodium diets that made every meal bland and joyless.

Seven years of vestibular therapy that never actually helped.

Seven years of being told "it's Ménière's, this is chronic, you'll manage it for life."

I did everything they asked.

When that didn't work, they sent me for more tests.

VNG test with those black goggles. Positive for Ménière's.

Audiogram. Slight hearing loss in my left ear. MRI. Normal. They said that confirmed it.

"Classic Ménière's," they said. "Your inner ear fluid is out of balance."

I felt broken. Like my body had turned against me.

Some days the ringing was so loud I couldn't hear my husband talking across the kitchen table.

That constant fullness in my ears. Like they were packed with cotton I couldn't pull out.

The dizziness wasn't severe spinning. Just a persistent, floating sensation that made me feel unsteady on my feet.

And every single morning, I'd wake up with my sinuses completely congested.

Pressure across my cheeks and forehead. Heavy. Thick. Never fully lifting.

But nobody connected those two things.

The sinus congestion was "just allergies."

The ear pressure and ringing? "That's your Ménière's."

Two separate problems, they said.

I stopped going to movies because the noise made the ringing unbearable.

I'd sit in restaurants and nod along to conversations I couldn't actually hear over the high-pitched screaming in my ears.

I stopped going to my book club because the room would tilt slightly whenever I stood up, and I couldn't follow the discussion over the ringing.

I planned every day around how congested I'd wake up and how loud the ringing would be.

And every doctor just nod…

Let's be honest, if you're still relying solely on the 0-5 Manual Muscle Test scale for anything beyond a basic neurological screen, you're leaving a mountain of valuable data on the table. It's subjective, has poor reliability for grades 4 and 5, and frankly, our patients deserve better.

Huge props to everyone who has already made the switch to objective strength testing with a handheld dynamometer (HHD). 👏 You're already ahead of the curve, getting real numbers to track progress and demonstrate value.

But are you getting the full picture?

We often get fixated on peak force and limb symmetry indexes. "The involved side is 20% weaker in peak isometric force." That's a great start, but it's not the end of the story.

Let's level up the conversation. 🚀

I'm talking about Rate of Force Development (RFD).

RFD measures how quickly an individual can generate force. It's essentially explosive strength, calculated as the change in force over the change in time (ΔF/Δt).

Think about its functional relevance: ✅ Preventing a fall after a stumble ✅ A soccer player's first step to the ball ✅ An ACL-R athlete's ability to "put the brakes on" during a cutting maneuver

An athlete might have perfectly symmetrical peak force, but if their RFD is significantly slower on their surgical side, you're looking at a potential performance deficit and an injury risk hiding in plain sight.

So, for all the clinicians out there already using HHDs:

Are you measuring Rate of Force Development in addition to peak force?
If so, what are you seeing? If not, what are the barriers? Let's discuss how we can continue to refine our assessments to get the best possible outcomes for our patients.

I saw 4 doctors about my PCOS facial hair. Not one of them asked the question that would've saved me 10 years of suffering….

I sat in my endocrinologist's office, gripping my purse so tightly my knuckles turned white.

This was my fourth doctor in 18 months.

The first one said "It's just PCOS. Try losing weight."

The second told me to "give the Metformin more time."

The third said, "Some women just have more facial hair. It's genetic."

The fourth said, "Have you considered laser? It's expensive but it works."

I was only 29.

Meanwhile, my husband mentioned he was self-conscious about his back hair at his annual physical and walked out with a referral to a dermatologist and three covered options.

One mention. One solution. No shame.

But me?

I was left to silently endure:
✘ Waking up at 5:30am to pluck before anyone saw me
✘ Stubble growing back by noon no matter how thoroughly I removed it
✘ Hair so thick and coarse it felt like wire pushing through my skin
✘ Dark spots spreading across my chin from years of trauma

=====

The nurse called my name.

I exhaled and stood slowly.

"Want me to come in with you?" my husband offered.

I shook my head. "I need to handle this alone."

As I walked down the hallway, one thought pulsed in my mind:

"Please let this doctor actually help me."

"How are you removing this hair?"

I blinked. "What do you mean?"

"Between treatments, between appointments. What's your daily method?"

"I pluck. Every morning. Sometimes twice a day."

She nodded slowly…

I've spent 9 years studying Blue Zones. These are the five places on earth where people routinely live past 100 — not in nursing homes, but actually healthy, sharp, and active well into their 90s and beyond.

Sardinia, Italy. Okinawa, Japan. Ikaria, Greece. Nicoya, Costa Rica. Loma Linda, California.

I've visited all five. Multiple trips. Exposed myself to things in these communities that researchers before me glossed over because they didn't fit the narrative.

—

I've worked in early childhood education for 11 years.

I've helped potty train hundreds of kids across three different daycares.

And I can tell you something that most parenting books won't.

I can predict within the first week which kids are going to train fast and which ones are going to struggle for months.

It has nothing to do with their personality.

It has to do with one thing.

—

Let me back up.

When I first started working in childcare, I assumed potty training was mostly about timing and temperament.

But somewhere around year three or four, I started noticing a pattern that I couldn't explain.

We'd get a class of ten toddlers starting the potty training transition around the same age.

And without fail, the class would split into two groups.

Group one would show potty awareness pretty quick, and group two don't have a care in the world

1280887800433310.caption: try-edenlabs.com
1280887800433310.copy:
I'm a parasitologist. I've spent 12 years studying parasites that live inside the human body. The first thing you learn in my field is that raw unpasteurized dairy is one of the most common sources of parasitic infection in humans.

Then I visited Russia where raw milk, unprocessed kefir, and fresh farmer’s cheese straight from the farm are consumed as casually as we drink tap water.

What I found there broke everything I thought I knew.

—

Let me back up.

I work in a university research lab. Doctors send me samples when they've run out of answers. Biopsies. Tissue sections. Stool specimens from patients who've been sick for years and nobody can figure out why.

By the time a sample hits my bench, I already know what the chart is going to say. Because it always says the same thing.

Patient presents with chronic bloating. Doctor's notes: IBS. Recommend dietary modification.

Patient returns. Fatigue that sleep doesn't fix. Doctor's notes: Chronic fatigue. Blood panel normal. Recommend exercise.

Patient returns. Waking up at 3am every night. Heart pounding. Can't fall back asleep. Doctor's notes: Sleep disruption. Likely stress-related. Prescribe sleep aid.

Patient returns. Brain fog. Forgetting words. Can't follow conversations. Doctor's notes: Consider cognitive evaluation.

Patient returns. Sugar cravings so intense they feel involuntary. Gaining weight. Doctor's notes: Discuss dietary discipline with patient.

Five visits. Five years. Five separate diagnoses. Five separate prescriptions.

Then someone finally sends the sample to me.

I prepare the slide. Look through the eyepiece. And in less than a minute I find what explains every single one of those visits.

Parasites.

Eggs. Clusters of them. Embedded deep in the tissue. Anchored into the intestinal lining.

Larvae. Some still moving. Tiny, pale, worm-like shapes twisting under the lens.

And surrounding everything, this thick, grayish coating so dense it hides the intestinal cells underneath.

Biofil…

990562923748937.copy:
After my husband died, my best friends excluded me from our annual trip to Japan. I went anyway. When their trip fell apart, they all frantically tried to reach me.

I did not pick up the phone.

I was in a garden in the mountains, on the third morning, drinking tea I hadn't asked for.

For ten years, Mark and I traveled with the same five couples. Every year, somewhere new. I'm the one who planned it. Always. I found the houses, the restaurants, the flights. I booked everything, organized the itineraries, handled the problems when they came. That was my role. For a decade.

Mark died in March.

Eight months later, someone in the group texts that this year's trip is Japan. Ten days. Kyoto, then the coast.

I'd already started researching. I had a folder. Ryokans, train schedules, a sushi counter in Kyoto that required a reservation four months out through a concierge service only available in Japanese. I was three weeks into the planning.

Then the message came from Melissa's phone.

"Hey Jen. So we've been talking as a group, and we think it might be better if this year's trip stays a couples thing. Japan is a LOT. The flights, the language barrier, the trains. We just want to make sure the trip runs smoothly for everyone."

Smoothly for everyone.

I read it twice.

Then I called her.

She answered on the second ring.

"Melissa. Talk to me."

A pause.

"It's just, Japan is complicated. International flights, connections, navigating a country where nothing is in English. Mark always handled the logistics for you two, and we just don't want you to be overwhelmed."

"Mark didn't handle the logistics. I did. For all of us. For ten years."

She stopped.

Long enough to answer the question without words.

Then her voice shifted. Warm in the specific way that arrives just before a difficult sentence.

It was the bumps that broke me first.

Not the hair.

The bumps.

Those angry red ingrown hairs that would swell up along my bikini line like tiny volcanoes. Some of them would get infected. Some would leave dark spots that lasted months.

My boyfriend never said anything, but I knew he saw them.

How could he not?

They were everywhere. Bikini line. Inner thighs. Even where my underwear sat.

I started avoiding intimacy just to avoid being seen.

========

Then came the stubble shadow...

Shave on Monday morning. Stubble by Monday night. Full regrowth by Tuesday.

I'd run my hand across my bikini line in the shower and feel it. Rough. Prickly. Like sandpaper.

I was shaving every single day. Sometimes twice.

My skin never had time to heal before I was dragging a razor across it again.

Another shower.
Another shave.
Another round of razor burn on skin that was already screaming.

========

And the dark spots?

One woman in a forum described it perfectly:

"It looks like I have a permanent shadow down there, even when I've just shaved."

That's exactly it.

Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation from years of shaving and waxing.

No amount of exfoliating fixed it.

Nothing faded it.

Just... dark patches on my most intimate skin.

========

My breaking point came on a trip to Ibiza with the girls.

Please STOP trying to fix your dog's allergies.
I know that sounds insane when you're watching your dog suffer. But hear me out.

Because what you're doing right now—the medications, the special foods, the endless vet visits—is like bailing water out of a sinking boat without plugging the hole.

Let me tell you what I wish someone had told me before I wasted $4,800 and 14 months going in circles.

It started small.

Just some scratching after being outside. A little redness on the belly. Nothing that seemed serious.

Then it got worse.

The scratching became constant. Hot spots appeared overnight. The ears started smelling like a brewery.

First vet visit: "Let's try Benadryl and see how it goes."

It didn't go well.

Second visit: "Okay, time for Apoquel. This should help."

It did help. For exactly 19 days. I know because I marked it on the calendar with a little celebration star.

Day 20, scratching came back full force.

Third visit: "We need to increase the dose."

Higher dose, higher price, same result two weeks later.

Fourth visit: "Let's switch to Cytopoint injections. More targeted approach."

$180 every two weeks became my new normal.

And you know what? It worked. Sort of. For a while.

But "a while" kept getting shorter.

Six weeks became four weeks became three weeks became "can we come in early, the itching is back."

Meanwhile, we tried everything else too.

Grain-free food. Then grain-in food. Then fish-based food. Then novel protein food that cost more per pound than my own groceries.

Allergy testing that showed sensitivity to basically everything that exists outdoors.

Probiotics. Fish oil. Coconut oil applied directly to the skin. Oatmeal baths every three days.

Every single thing worked for about two weeks.

Then right back to square one.

The worst part wasn't the money, though yeah, $4,800 was crushing.

The worst part was the hope cycle.

At 2am, three weeks after my doctor told me there was nothing wrong with me, I sat at the kitchen table and began writing letters for my children to open on their eighteenth birthdays.

Because I was certain. Not scared. Certain. I was not going to be alive to see them grow up.

I'm Sarah. I'm 39. I live in Bristol with my husband Tom and our two, Lily who is seven and Jack who is ten.

I am writing this for the woman who is sitting up tonight, sure that something is seriously wrong with her, while every doctor tells her she is fine.

I was her for eighteen months. Please read all of it.

It crept in so slowly I explained it away for nearly a year.

First the exhaustion. Not normal mum tired. I slept a full night and woke up like I had been hit by a bus.

Then the bloating. Flat when I woke up. By the afternoon I looked five months pregnant, undoing the button of my jeans under my jumper at the school gates so no one would see.

Then the brain fog. One Friday I forgot to collect Lily. The school rang me. My seven year old was the last child standing in an empty playground while her mother sat at home in a daze. I have never felt shame like it.

Then the 3am waking, every night. The sugar cravings I hid. My hair coming out in the shower. Half a stone gone without trying.

So I did the right thing. I went to the doctor.

GP one: "You're a busy mum. You're run down. Try getting more rest."

GP two: "Your bloods are normal. Probably perimenopause. Have you thought about antidepressants?"

I knew the difference between low and what was happening to me. I said no.

Private GP, two hundred pounds: "Adrenal fatigue. Try this magnesium."

Gastroenterologist, three hundred and fifty pounds: "It's IBS. Eat more fibre."

I ate more fibre. The bloating got so bad I could not stand up straight.

By then I was convinced they had missed something terminal. That is the honest truth. I lay awake doing the maths of who would take the kids to school, whether Tom would cope, what I need…

I just want a bra that doesn't hurt my ribs and supports my breasts.

That's it. That's the whole brief. And every bra company in Britain has failed her on exactly that for thirty years.

You thought it was sizing. You tried going up a band. Going down a cup. Going wireless. Going wired.

You've been fitted. Refitted. Gone up a band. Down a cup. Tried wireless. Tried wired. Spent £40 at M&S. £55 at John Lewis. Another £30 on something with 4,000 five-star reviews that swore blind it would feel like nothing.

It still hurt 30 minutes after putting it on!

Not a little. That slow, building crush under the band. The kind that starts as an ache and ends with you pressing your palm flat against your ribs just to get through the afternoon. The kind that means the first thing you do when you get through your front door isn't take your shoes off.

It's reach behind your back and unclasp time.

You've done that sh*t for DECADES. And somewhere along the way you decided it was just you. Wrong size. Sensitive ribs. Something wrong with your body.

Newsflash, it isn't you. And you're not the only one who taught it IS you. But it isn't.

Most bra band sit on your lower ribs 8, 9, and 10. Unlike the ribs above them, these ones aren't anchored to your sternum. They float. They flex with every breath you take.

Ribs 8, 9, and 10 are surrounded by intercostal nerves that carry sensation across your entire trunk. When a rigid band presses into that zone for hours, those nerves get crushed.

And every hour a rigid band sits there, it presses into the nerves running between them. Those nerves carry sensation across your entire trunk. When they get compressed for hours, the pain doesn't just stay local. It radiates. Your breathing goes shallow. Your body starts bracing against the very thing you're wearing.

That's not a sizing problem. That's anatomy.

And refitting won't fix it either. Because the woman measuring you at M&S doesn't know about floating ribs. Nobody trained her on tha…

I've been a pediatric nurse for 18 years. I've watched hundreds of parents come in worried about their child's height. I told every single one of them to "just be patient." Then I watched a boy I'd known since he was 8 lose every ounce of confidence he had while we all said those words. When my own son started falling behind, I refused to follow the same script. By the end of this you're going to understand exactly why, and what I found instead.

I've been a pediatric nurse for 18 years.

In that time I've seen hundreds of parents sit across from me, growth chart in hand, asking why their child isn't catching up. But the ones that stayed with me long after they left the office weren't the ones asking about percentiles. They were the ones telling me their child had stopped wanting to go to school. That their son came home crying because someone called him "baby" again. That the outgoing kid they raised had gone quiet and they didn't know how to get him back.

I've watched parents do everything right. Extra milk. Protein at every meal. Multivitamins. Early bedtimes. Pep talks every night about how height doesn't define you. Some of them bought NuBest or TruHeight and gave it to their kids for months, sometimes years. Some enrolled their kids in sports for confidence. Had them in therapy. Talked to the school about the teasing. Did everything they could for their child's body AND their child's mind.

And I've watched too many of those children stay at the same percentile year after year, getting more withdrawn and more defeated every month, until the growth plates closed and the window was gone.

I've sat with those parents afterward. I've heard the guilt in their voices. "Should we have done something different? Did we wait too long?"

I know exactly what that path looks like.

And then I watched it happen to a boy named Jacob.

Jacob was 8 when I first met him. His mother brought him in because he was noticeably shorter than his classmates. 7th percentile. She was wo…

1373809467525501.copy:
I drove to a breeder's house in rural Yorkshire six months after Max died. I wasn't there as a vet. I was there as a woman who lost her German Shepherd and wasn't ready to live in a house without one.

The breeder's name was Joan. She'd been breeding German Shepherds for 28 years. Her name came up in every working-dog circle I'd ever been in. "If you want a Shepherd with good hips, you go to Joan." I'd heard it from clients. From colleagues. From the rescue community. Everyone said the same thing: Joan's dogs keep walking.

I pulled into her driveway expecting a kennel operation. What I found was a farmhouse with 6 adult Shepherds lying on the porch in the sun.

I need to tell you what those 6 dogs looked like because it stopped me before I got out of my car.

They were healthy in a way I'd never seen in my own practice. Coats shining. Eyes bright. But it was how they moved. When I closed my car door, all six stood up. No hesitation. No slow rising. No stiff back legs. No sliding on the wood decking.

Six large German Shepherds getting up simultaneously, and it was effortless.

I treat Shepherds every day. I know what a 41-kilogram dog looks like when it tries to stand.

The oldest was 14.

Fourteen years old.

I've been a veterinary surgeon for 10 years. I have never treated a German Shepherd who lived to 14 with fully functioning back legs. The median mobility decline in my practice starts around 7.

This woman had a 14-year-old Shepherd walking down the porch steps looking better than most 5-year-olds I see in my consulting room.

Joan came out. She was maybe 70. Strong. Direct.

She shook my hand and looked at me the way breeders look at people who might take one of their puppies home. Evaluating. Deciding if I was good enough.

We sat on the porch. The 14-year-old, whose name was Ruth, put her head on Joan's foot and went to sleep.

I couldn't help myself.

I forgot I was there to buy a puppy.

I said: "How is that dog 14 and still walking like that?"

Joan did…

2331699980972944.copy:
Last month I went to Greece with four girlfriends, and a 74-year-old woman at our hotel made all five of us feel invisible.

Last month I went to Greece with my four closest girlfriends.

We'd been planning it for two years.

A week in Santorini for Sarah's 55th birthday.

Five women who've known each other since our kids were in kindergarten together, finally doing the trip we'd been promising ourselves.

We arrived exhausted and excited and immediately changed into our swimsuits and went to the pool.

That's where we saw her.

Seventy-four years old.

We found out later because Diane asked directly.

Diane has never had a filter, and we've all stopped trying to install one.

She was at the far end of the pool on a lounge chair.

Not hiding.

Not positioned strategically.

Just there, the way someone is there when they've long since stopped thinking about how they look to other people.

Skin firm.

Posture easy.

Arms that looked like they belonged to a woman who used them regularly and expected them to cooperate.

She glowed in a way that had nothing to do with the Greek sun.

She'd clearly just arrived at the pool the same as us.

The five of us looked at each other without saying anything.

Sarah said it first.

"Is she on Ozempic?"

We all laughed.

Then we all kept watching her.

Here's who we five are.

Sarah.

Fifty-five this trip.

The reason we came.

Personal trainer three times a week.

Has been on HRT for two years.

Diane.

Fifty-four.

The one who asks the questions nobody else will.

Collagen supplements every morning without fail.

Cut out alcohol entirely last January.

Meg.

Fifty-three.

Runs half marathons.

Follows an anti-inflammatory diet.

Sees a functional medicine doctor every quarter.

Rachel.

Fifty-two.

The youngest of us.

Has been doing everything right since she turned forty-five because she saw what happened to her mother at sixty and decided she wasn't going to let that happen to her.

And me.

Fifty-three.

SPF every morning.

Re…

1381458963944150.caption: try-edenlabs.com
1381458963944150.copy:
Three months after my divorce, I found out my best friends went on a two-week trip to Italy without me. Not because they told me. Because my best friends posted photos all over Instagram.

Cassie and I have been best friends for twenty years. She and Greg, Mike and Pam, Dave and Rachel, three couples plus Mark and me.

For sixteen years, we cruised the Mediterranean together every September. I researched the ports. Found the excursions. Booked the restaurants. Mark handled the logistics at the terminals.

Mark and I divorced fourteen months ago. He'd been having an affair with a woman from his gym. She was 34.

After the papers were signed, the calls came constantly.

Cassie checking in.

Pam dropping off wine.

Everyone saying "we're here for you, whatever you need."

By month three, the calls slowed down.

By month six, they stopped.

Then I open Instagram on a Tuesday morning. And there they are. All six of them.

At a café in Florence. Cassie's holding a glass of wine and grinning. The caption: "The crew does Italy."

The crew.

Without me.

I called Cassie that afternoon.

"Oh, Susan." That voice. The one that sounds like warmth but lands like a verdict.

"We didn't want to make things awkward. It was sort of last-minute. And honestly, we didn't think you'd be comfortable. You know, with everything you've been going through."

Everything I've been going through.

She kept going.

"And Italy is a lot. The trains, the walking, the cobblestones everywhere. You've just seemed so worn down lately. We didn't think you could manage it alone."

I sat there and listened.

"It was for your own good, Susan. We didn't want you to be overwhelmed."

Two weeks later, they're all back. Tanned. Full of stories.

And Cassie calls me.

"Susan, I have exciting news. We're doing our annual cruise in September. Mediterranean. And we'd love for you to help plan the itinerary. You always find those incredible hidden restaurants and those excursions nobody else knows about. You're so …

Children who potty train after 32 months are 3x more likely to develop chronic constipation, urinary incontinence, or daytime accidents.

I found this out two weeks after my daughter's 4th birthday.

While she's still in diapers.

My name is Kate. I'm 29 years old.

And I'm genuinely terrified I've waited too long.

We've been "trying" to potty train for 18 months.

I put trying in quotes because I don't even know if you can call it trying anymore.

We did the 3-day method at 2 and a half. Failed.

Tried again at 3. Failed.

Tried rewards, timers, special underwear, potty seats. All failed.

Every time, same pattern. A few days of minimal progress, then total shutdown.

Back to diapers.

Her pediatrician kept saying "some kids take longer. Don't stress."

So I didn't stress.

I figured she'd get there eventually.

But last week, I got the kindergarten enrollment packet in the mail.

There was a highlighted section at the bottom:

"All children must be fully toilet trained to attend kindergarten. No exceptions."

Kindergarten starts in 5 months.

And my daughter still can't tell me when she needs to go.

So I really wanted to find a solution and needed it FAST.

I was up late googling "4 year old not potty trained" for probably the hundredth time.

And I found an actual study that is mind blowing...

"Children who were toilet trained after 32 months old had significantly higher rates of urge incontinence (daytime wetting and bedwetting) between ages 4-12."

My daughter is 48 months old.

That's 16 months past the 32-month mark.

I kept reading.

The study said kids who train late are more likely to have accidents and bladder control issues in preschool and elementary school.

Not just during training. For years after.

Because the bladder learns through practice.

If toddlers ignore the urge for too long because they're in diapers, it creates bad habits that persist.

3038899036497820.caption: upairy.com
3038899036497820.copy:
In Vietnam, the average age of potty training is 9 months old. (I promise I’m not making this up - it’s a documented cultural norm) 

In the US, it has crept up to 36+ months. 

Are American babies biologically different? No. 

Are Vietnamese moms wizards? No. 

The difference is simply what we wrap our kids butts in. 

And I sat there staring at these stats, realizing I was 2 years behind a standard I didn't even know existed.

—

So for the past 14 months everyone kept telling me "wait until she's ready."

My pediatrician gave me this whole checklist of readiness signs to watch for.

Stays dry for 2 hours, shows interest in the potty, can follow simple instructions.

So I waited and watched while she stayed in pull-ups.

And every few weeks I'd think "okay maybe she's ready now?"

But there was always one sign missing so I'd tell myself just wait a little longer.

Month after month after month.

Meanwhile she's 3 and a half and I'm watching 2-year-olds at the playground already trained.

And I'd think "what am I doing wrong?"

But everyone said don't rush it, she'll tell you when she's ready.

So I kept waiting.

For 14 months.

While she stayed comfortable in disposables that I changed 6 times a day.

—

So last week I was scrolling Reddit at 11 PM trying to figure out how the heck they do it so early. 

And I saw this comment that connected the dots for me. 

It turns out, we used to be almost as fast as them.

"92% of children in 1957 were toilet trained by 18 months." 

Then: "The current average is 35 months for girls, 39 months for boys." 

And I'm staring at my phone thinking... wait, WHAT? 

So the US used to be like Vietnam, but now we're 2 years behind?

So I went down a complete rabbit hole that night. 

I found data from the American Academy of Family Physicians. 

In the 1940s, we were training almost as early as they do in Vietnam. 

Now it starts between 21 and 36 months.

And only 40 to 60 percent of kids even COMPLETE training by 36 months…

Please STOP trying to fix your dog's allergies.

I know that sounds insane when you're watching your dog suffer. But hear me out.

Because what you're doing right now — the medications, the special foods, the endless vet visits — is like bailing water out of a sinking boat without plugging the hole.

Let me tell you what I wish someone had told me before I wasted $4,800 and 14 months going in circles.

It started small.

Just some scratching after being outside. A little redness on the belly. Nothing that seemed serious.

Then it got worse.

The scratching became constant. Hot spots appeared overnight. The ears started smelling like a brewery.

First vet visit: "Let's try Benadryl and see how it goes."

It didn't go well.

Second visit: "Okay, time for Apoquel. This should help."

It did help. For exactly 19 days. I know because I marked it on the calendar with a little celebration star.

Day 20, scratching came back full force.

Third visit: "We need to increase the dose."

Higher dose, higher price, same result two weeks later.

Fourth visit: "Let's switch to Cytopoint injections. More targeted approach."

$180 every two weeks became my new normal.

And you know what? It worked. Sort of. For a while.

But "a while" kept getting shorter.

Six weeks became four weeks became three weeks became "can we come in early, the itching is back."

Meanwhile, we tried everything else too.

Grain-free food. Then grain-in food. Then fish-based food. Then novel protein food that cost more per pound than my own groceries.

Allergy testing that showed sensitivity to basically everything that exists outdoors.

Probiotics. Fish oil. Coconut oil applied directly to the skin. Oatmeal baths every three days.

Every single thing worked for about two weeks.

Then right back to square one.

The worst part wasn't the money, though yeah, $4,800 was crushing.

The worst part was the hope cycle.

New treatment → improvement → "finally, we've got it!" → symptoms return → devastation…

My 97-year-old host in Sardinia, Italy eats cheese every morning, drinks red wine every night, has never taken a supplement, and hasn't seen a doctor in over 20 years. When I asked her secret, her answer had nothing to do with diet.

I spent three weeks in Sardinia last spring doing research on Blue Zones. If you don't know what that is, it's one of five places on earth where people routinely live past 100 years old.

Not just alive in a nursing home, but actually healthy, sharp, and active well into their 90s and beyond.

Sardinia has one of the highest concentrations of centenarians on the planet. And unlike most places where women outlive men by a decade, here the men live just as long. Shepherds in their 90s still walking steep mountain trails every single morning.

I stayed with a woman named Maria through a homestay program.

She's 97 years old. Still herds her goats every morning before sunrise. Still makes her own cheese by hand. Still walks mountain paths that would leave most 40-year-olds gasping.

And here's what made no sense. She breaks every health rule Americans follow. All of them.

She eats cheese and bread at every meal. Full fat. Nothing low-calorie. Nothing measured.

She drinks red wine every single night. Not a small glass. A real pour.

She has never stepped foot in a gym. Never done a workout. Never counted a step. The only exercise she gets is walking her goats up the mountain and tending her garden.

She has never taken a vitamin. Never taken a supplement. Never taken a pill of any kind.

She hasn't seen a doctor in over 20 years. Not because she can't afford it. Because she hasn't needed to.

She eats unpasteurized cheese she presses with her bare hands. Drinks milk straight from the goat. Handles livestock every day and doesn't wash her hands before making breakfast.

742321081988365.caption: upairy.com
742321081988365.copy:
My best friend's daughter potty trained in 3 days, while mine took over a year. Here's what we did differently...

Because when I look back at that year with my daughter, I realize I made it SO much harder than it needed to be.

My friend Melissa and I had our daughters three days apart.

We were pregnant together, went through labor at the same hospital, raised them side by side.

I thought "how hard can potty training be?"

I'd seen so many moms online do it in a weekend. Heck, there's even a method called "3 day potty training."

Oh boy was I wrong....

---

Last spring, Melissa and I decided to start potty training together.

We picked the same weekend. Made it fun. Did it side by side.

I bought the cute potty. I bought the sticker charts. And I stocked up on pull-ups because I HATE changing diapers and didn't want pee on my rugs.

And that was the decision that wasted over a year of our lives.

Day 3, Melissa texts me: "Mia went twice today! She's getting it!"

Day 3 for us? My daughter Lily had 10 accidents and screamed at the potty.

I texted back: "That's amazing! We're still figuring it out."

I figured okay, some kids are faster. Lily will get there.

Week two, Melissa: "She's basically got it. Maybe one accident a day."

Week two for us? Still 8-10 accidents daily.

I stopped updating her.

Month later, we met at the park.

Mia ran up and said "Mommy I need to potty."

They walked to the bathroom together. Done.

Lily had TWO accidents while we were there.

I watched Melissa's face. She was trying so hard not to look surprised.

On the drive home, I felt so defeated.

Same age. Same start time. Why did Mia train in days and Lily didn't train in months?

And I had no idea why.

---

So I kept trying. For a year.

Three-day method. Rewards. Timers every 20 minutes.

Nothing worked.

She'd say "I don't need to go" and pee two minutes later.

I thought she was stubborn. I thought she "wasn't ready."

Month eight, our pediatrician said "some kids just take lo…

A nurse pressed two fingers into my wife's stomach, held them there, and said, "There is something moving under my hand and it is not her pulse." Then she walked out of the room to get somebody else.

That was appointment nine. Nine appointments in fourteen months, and it was the first time anyone had actually put a hand on her.

I'm Mark, I'm 47, and I live in Leeds. My wife Claire is 44. We have Ellie, who is thirteen, and Sam, who is nine.

I am writing this for the bloke who is lying next to a woman who keeps telling him that something is wrong inside her, while every letter from the hospital says she is fine. I did not believe her properly for about a year. I have to live with that.

It came on so slowly that we both had an excuse ready for every bit of it.

The bloating was first. Claire would come down in the morning in her pyjamas with a flat stomach, and by six in the evening she looked six months gone. She started sitting down to her tea with her jeans unbuttoned under the table and her jumper pulled down over the top. She thought I had not noticed. I had noticed for months and said nothing because I did not know what to say.

Then the tiredness, and it was not tiredness like mine at the end of a long week. She would sleep nine hours and come down grey. She told me once it was not being tired, it was being emptied out. She would sit on the settee at four o'clock on a Saturday and that was her finished for the day. Ellie learned to bring her a blanket without being asked, and that is the detail I think about now.

Then the fog. Claire does payroll, she has done it for eighteen years, she is the one who does our tax return and can add up a shop in her head. She started losing the thread halfway through her own sentences. She rang me from the Morrisons car park one Thursday because she could not remember what she had gone in for, and she had the receipt in her hand while she was asking me.

Then the three in the morning thing. Near enough on the hour, every n…

2018538128736893.copy:
I Ordered TheraPet on a Monday Night...
And Then I Panicked.

Did I just waste $75?
What if it doesn’t work?
What if nothing happens?

If you just ordered...
Or you’re about to order...
Let me tell you exactly what happened.

Day by day.
So you know what to expect.

It Arrived Thursday Afternoon

Four business days.

The box was smaller than I expected.
Three white diffusers. Simple instructions.

I read the instructions twice.

“Plug in areas where your dog spends the most time.”
“Results typically within 3–5 days.”

Okay.

I plugged one in the living room outlet.
Right next to where my dog paces constantly.

The second I plugged it in, something happened.

My dog walked over.
Sniffed it.
Tilted his head.
Then walked away.

I thought: Well, at least he noticed it.

I plugged the second one in my bedroom.
Where he sleeps and barks at night.

Same thing.
He came over. Sniffed. Walked away.

The third one went in the kitchen.
By the door where he pees every single time I leave.

Again... he sniffed it for a few seconds.
Then just... went and laid down.

That Was Thursday Evening

I didn’t expect anything to happen immediately.
The instructions said 3–5 days.

So I just waited.

That night?
He still paced before bed.
Still barked once at a noise outside.

I went to bed thinking: Okay... give it time.

Friday – Day 1

Woke up.
Checked the floor.

One pee puddle in the hallway.
Same as always.

I cleaned it up.
Took him outside.

Left for the grocery store for an hour.
Came home expecting pee by the door.

No pee.

I checked twice.
Nothing.

Okay. Maybe a fluke.

That evening, a delivery driver came to the door.
My dog usually goes crazy.

Barking.
Running to the door.
Won’t stop until they leave.

This time?
He looked up.
Didn’t bark.
Just... looked.

I stood there shocked.

What just happened?

Saturday – Day 2

Woke up.
Checked the floor.

One small pee spot near the kitchen.
Not his usual three or four puddles.
Just one.

And it was smaller.…

Didn't stop. Didn't look down. Didn't notice.

She just kept stacking them while a puddle formed under her.

She looked up at me. Confused.

Like she genuinely had no idea what I was talking about.

Did the 3-day method. Cleared a long weekend. Read all the guides.

Day one was rough but I expected that.

Day three, complete shutdown. Refused to sit. Had a full meltdown.

A little progress then total resistance.

So I tried rewards. Sticker charts. Special treats. Extra screen time.

She'd use the potty once to get the reward then nothing for days.

And the whole time I'm watching her have these accidents where she just doesn't know.

Like she'd be standing there. Pee literally running down her leg.

And she wouldn't notice until I told her.

Here's what makes it even more confusing.

Her younger brother trained at 2 and a half.

No drama. No resistance.

One day he asked to try the potty. Two weeks later he was done.

Now he tells me when he needs to go.

1656846428840123.caption: trycanislabs.com
1656846428840123.copy:
I walk my dog at 5:30 in the morning.
 
Not because I like mornings.
 
Because that's the only time the neighborhood is empty enough that I don't have to brace myself.
 
No kids on bikes. No dogs being walked. No joggers coming around corners.
 
Just me, Stella, and forty-five minutes of actually breathing normally.
 
Then I get home, and I watch my neighbor Sarah leave with her Labrador at 8 AM. They walk straight through the park. Stop to talk to people. Let other dogs say hello. Come back forty minutes later.
 
And I don't say anything. I just close the blinds.
 
Because I know what that walk would look like with Stella.
 
The second she sees another dog — 50 feet, 80 feet, doesn't matter — her whole body changes. She locks on. She pulls toward them or pulls away from them. She barks and lunges so hard the leash cuts into my hand.
 
I've been knocked down twice.
 
Once on the sidewalk. Once on a trail when she saw a dog come around a bend.

There are 7 million kids in America with an ADHD diagnosis right now. 3.3 million of their parents are holding a prescription they refuse to fill.

I'm one of them. And until six weeks ago, I thought I was failing my son.

His name is Theo. He's 9. He was diagnosed at 6.

And the way out of it was not the thing I expected.

Theo is a sweet kid. Wild and funny, obsessed with dinosaurs, capable of explaining the entire plot of every Pixar movie in chronological order.

He's also been melting down at the dinner table since he was 4.

Not toddler tantrums. Real, plate-throwing, screaming-into-a-pillow, can't-be-reasoned-with meltdowns. Over the broccoli touching the pasta. Over losing a video game. Over a sock that "feels weird."

His pediatrician diagnosed him with ADHD when he was 6. She handed me a prescription for a 5mg dose of a stimulant. I sat in my car in the parking lot and cried for forty minutes before driving home with that prescription folded in my purse.

I never filled it.

So I decided I'd do it the natural way. I started buying supplements.

I bought fish oil — the high-DHA kind, the Nordic Naturals one for kids, the one all the parenting forums recommended. Three months. Nothing.

And Then I Panicked.

Did I just waste $75?

What if nothing happens?

Or you’re about to order...
Let me tell you exactly what happened.

Day by day.

Three white diffusers. Simple instructions.

“Results typically within 3–5 days.”

Okay.

I plugged one in the living room outlet.
Right next to where my dog paces constantly.

Sniffed it.
Tilted his head.
Then walked away.

I thought: Well, at least he noticed it.

I plugged the second one in my bedroom.
Where he sleeps and barks at night.

Same thing.
He came over. Sniffed. Walked away.

The third one went in the kitchen.
By the door where he pees every single time I leave.

Again... he sniffed it for a few seconds.
Then just... went and laid down.

I didn’t expect anything to happen immediately.
The instructions said 3–5 days.

So I just waited.

That night?

I stood there shocked.

What just happened?

Not his usual three or four puddles.
Just one.

I drop my three dogs off at daycare twice a week. The owner told me ultrasonic flea repellers are a scam.

Last Tuesday, she pulled me aside and asked why my dogs are the only ones without fleas.

The daycare owner, Michelle, has been running Happy Tails for eleven years. She sees forty to sixty dogs every single day. She's seen every flea treatment, every collar, every gadget dog owners swear by.

And for two years, every time I mentioned ultrasonic pest repellers, she'd roll her eyes.

"They don't work," she'd say. "I've had clients try them. Their dogs always come back with fleas."

So I listened to her.

I used the monthly chemical drops she recommended. Applied them to my three dogs—Max, Bella, and Cooper—every thirty days like clockwork.

The fleas never fully went away.

Last spring, it got bad. Max was scratching himself raw. Bella had bald patches behind her ears. Cooper wouldn't stop biting at his back legs.

I went to Costco and bought a 3-pack of ultrasonic pest repellers anyway. Fifty-two dollars. I figured I had nothing to lose.

Michelle noticed them in my bag at drop-off the next week.

"What are those?"

"Ultrasonic repellers," I said.

She shook her head. "Save your money. I've seen dozens of clients try those. Not one of them worked. The dogs always come back here with fleas."

"Yeah, well, the drops aren't working either."

She looked at Max's raw patches. She knew I was right.

I plugged the units in. Living room, bedroom, kitchen.

Nothing happened.

Week one, no change. Week two, maybe fewer fleas. By week three, they were back worse than before.

Michelle didn't say anything at the next drop-off. She didn't have to. I could see it in her face when she checked my dogs in and found fleas on all three of them.

I threw the units in a drawer and went back to the chemical drops.

Four months later, Michelle pulled me aside at pick-up.

"Can I talk to you for a minute?"

I thought something was wrong. Maybe one of my dogs had gotten into a figh…

I'm a doctor with chronic insomnia. I refused sleeping pills for 2 years. Here's what finally got me sleeping through the night.

I've been a doctor for 26 years, and sleep problems are something I see in patients constantly. 

The bags under the eyes. 

The ones who haven't had a proper night's sleep in months. 

The ones lying awake at 3 AM scrolling their phone because they're too wired to drift off. 

I've watched countless people end up on Ambien, Lunesta, or low-dose anti-anxiety meds just to get through the night.

About two years ago, it happened to me.

I'm 59. Two grand kids. Husband. Full-time shifts at the hospital plus all the chaos of normal family life. I used to sleep fine. Then something shifted. I'd lie in bed completely exhausted, but my brain refused to switch off. I'd run through tomorrow's to-do list. Re-live conversations from work. Worry about the kids. By the time I finally drifted off it was 1 AM, and I'd be up again at 4 with my jaw clenched and my shoulders somewhere near my ears.

Mornings were a write-off. I'd snap at my kids over nothing. I'd forget words mid-sentence. I'd drink three coffees just to function until lunch, then crash again at 3 PM. My husband told me I'd started grinding my teeth in my sleep so loudly it was waking him up.

I went to my GP. She offered me Ambien. I smiled politely and said I'd think about it.

But I knew I wasn't going to take it. I've watched too many patients become dependent on it. The next-day grogginess where they're walking around like zombies. The weird sleepwalking stories. The fact that you can't just stop taking it without your sleep getting even worse than before. I wasn't about to trade one nightmare for another.

So I just dealt with it. Melatonin. Valerian root tea. CBD oil. ZzzQuil on really bad nights. Cut out caffeine after 2 PM. Magnesium powder from the chemist. Lavender pillow spray. Every sleep podcast and meditation app on my phone. Nothing really worked, but what else was I suppos…

2139610950294089.caption: nirapet.com
2139610950294089.copy:
My Vet Pushed Apoquel for 14 Months. I Kept Saying Not Yet. Here's What Happened to Her Itching.

I'm not a vet. I'm not a dog trainer. I'm a 58-year-old woman who works the front desk at a dental office in Ohio and has loved exactly four dogs in her life.

This is about the fourth one. Her name is Luna. 

She's a six-year-old yellow lab, and for fourteen months I watched her claw herself raw while my vet told me, at every single visit, that it was time to put her on Apoquel.

I kept saying not yet.

I want to tell you why I held out for fourteen months, and what finally stopped the scratching, because I needed someone to tell me this a year ago and nobody did.

It started small. A little scratching after dinner. I figured it was fleas, treated her, moved on.

But it didn't stop. It got worse.

By spring she was waking me up at 2 AM — that frantic thump-thump-thump of a back leg going at her ribs, then the licking. 

The endless licking. Her belly went from pink to angry red. The fur on her paws turned rust-colored and then just came off. 

Bald patches. Hot spots erupting under her chin every couple of weeks, weeping and raw.

I'd had her since she was a puppy. The dog who used to flip onto her back the second I sat on the floor, begging for a belly rub. 

Now if I touched her belly she'd flinch and go straight back to licking the spot I'd touched. Like I'd hurt her.

That was the part that broke me. I couldn't even pet my own dog.

As the founder of FullForce, I still think about how close our GM engine failure came with my son still in the truck.

He'd climbed out five minutes earlier. Football practice. I was driving home alone when I heard the tick.

Fourteen years, I'd fixed this exact failure in other families' trucks. Silverados, Sierras, Tahoes, Yukons, Suburbans, Escalades.

I'd never once let myself think about who might be riding in the ones that failed on the road, not in a driveway.

Then it was my own truck, and for the first time it wasn't a stranger's kid I was picturing.

My truck. A 2015 Chevrolet Silverado LT, 5.3 V8, bought new. 57,300 miles.

I checked the odometer three times in the driveway. Not because I doubted the number. Because I was still shaking a little.

Lifter failure. I knew before I even popped the hood.

I've diagnosed this exact failure more times than I can count. I never thought I'd be doing the math on my own truck, five minutes after my own son got out of it.

Here's the part that actually scares me.

There's no warning light. No time to plan around it. It happens wherever you happen to be, whoever happens to be riding with you.

Active Fuel Management. AFM. GM's had it in every V6 and V8 they build since 2007.

It shuts down half your cylinders while you cruise, to save a mile or two per gallon. That's the entire trade.

The lifters that make it work carry a tiny locking pin. That pin locks and unlocks hundreds of times a drive, thousands of times a week, for as long as you own the truck.

GM's own service bulletins, PIP5259 and PIP5776, document exactly what happens when it finally gives out.

Mine had been cycling like that for 57,300 miles before the pin let go and took the camshaft with it.

I do my own oil changes. Full synthetic, every interval, logged.

My friend came over last week and watched my cat for like five minutes. Then she looked at me and said, "Does she ever actually... do anything?"

She wakes up. Eats. Stares out the window for a while. Goes back to sleep. Same spot on the couch every single time. That's her entire day. Every day.
